chapters.title: Chapter 3: When Country Risk Turns Into Crisis

lessons.title: The Anatomy of a Sovereign Debt Crisis: Warning Signs and Triggers

children.text: Chapter 2 closed with a warning: markets often reprice a country's risk well before rating agencies catch up. This chapter is about what happens when that repricing turns into an actual crisis. Sovereign debt crises look different on the surface, Mexico in 1994, Asia in 1997, Argentina in 2001, Greece in 2010, Sri Lanka in 2022, but strip away the local detail and almost every one of them follows the same four-stage anatomy. Learning that anatomy here means the Sri Lanka case study in the next lesson will feel familiar rather than foreign.
The Common Anatomy: Four Stages of a Sovereign Debt Crisis

body.caption: How a Sovereign Debt Crisis Typically Unfolds

cells: 1. Building Vulnerability
A country accumulates risk over years, often while growth still looks fine on the surface
Twin deficits, rising foreign-currency debt, a currency that looks stronger than fundamentals justify
2. Trigger Event
An external or domestic shock exposes the vulnerability that was quietly building
A global rate hiking cycle, a commodity price spike, a pandemic, a political misstep
3. Loss of Confidence
Investors reprice risk fast, well ahead of formal rating actions, as covered in the last lesson
Widening bond spreads and CDS, sharp currency depreciation, foreign capital outflows
4. Crisis Point
Reserves run critically low, debt cannot be rolled over on affordable terms, the government is forced to act
Import cover collapses, capital controls imposed, default, restructuring, or an IMF programme

body.text: Notice how much of Stage 1 can look completely unremarkable at the time. GDP growth can be healthy, the stock market can be rallying, and headlines can be positive, all while twin deficits and foreign-currency exposure quietly build in the background. Sovereign crises rarely arrive without warning. They arrive without anyone paying attention to warnings that, in hindsight, were sitting in plain sight in the data this course has already covered.

children.text: The Warning Signs Analysts Actually Watch

markDefs.definition: A country running a fiscal deficit and a current account deficit at the same time, meaning the government is spending more than it earns and the country as a whole is spending more abroad than it earns from abroad. Both gaps typically need to be financed by foreign capital inflows.

children.text: Analysts return to a small set of metrics again and again when screening for building vulnerability.

are the starting point: a country simultaneously running a large fiscal deficit and a large current account deficit is financing two gaps at once, usually with foreign capital, which is exactly the kind of capital that can leave fastest when sentiment turns.

markDefs.definition: The number of months of a country's imports that its forex reserves could pay for if all other capital inflows suddenly stopped. A commonly cited rule of thumb treats less than three months as a danger zone.

children.text: Two more specific rules of thumb come up constantly in crisis analysis.

measures how many months of imports a country's forex reserves could fund if every other source of foreign currency dried up overnight; three months is widely treated as a minimum adequacy threshold, and many countries target well above that as a comfortable buffer. Separately, the Greenspan-Guidotti rule, proposed after the 1997-98 Asian Financial Crisis, holds that a country's forex reserves should at least equal its short-term external debt, the portion maturing within a year, so that it could theoretically pay off every near-term foreign-currency obligation without needing to borrow a single new dollar. Breach both of these thresholds at once and a country is in genuinely dangerous territory.

stats.label: Import Cover Danger Threshold
stats.context: A widely cited rule of thumb for minimum reserve adequacy

stats.label: Greenspan-Guidotti Rule
stats.context: Reserves should cover all foreign-currency debt maturing within a year

markDefs.definition: A large volume of a country's debt maturing within a short window, concentrating rollover risk. Even a country with a manageable total debt-to-GDP ratio can face a crisis if too much of that debt matures at once, especially into a hostile market.

children.text: A third, related signal is maturity concentration, sometimes called a

: a large share of debt bunched into a narrow maturity window. Recall from Chapter 1 that India deliberately manages a long weighted average maturity on its G-Secs, around 11 to 12 years, precisely to avoid this kind of concentration. Countries that borrowed heavily in shorter-dated foreign-currency instruments do not have that luxury, and a debt wall approaching at the exact moment reserves are thin and market sentiment has soured is close to the textbook setup for a default.
Triggers: What Actually Lights the Fuse
Vulnerability can sit quietly for years without becoming a crisis. It usually takes a trigger, and triggers tend to fall into two broad categories.

External triggers arrive from outside the country entirely. A US Federal Reserve rate hiking cycle raises the return available on safe dollar assets, pulling capital out of riskier emerging markets that had been reliant on cheap foreign funding, a dynamic sometimes called the 'taper tantrum' effect after a milder 2013 episode. A commodity price shock hits oil or food importing countries especially hard, widening their current account and fiscal gaps in one move. A global risk-off event, like the 2008 financial crisis or the 2020 pandemic, can shut off capital markets to weaker credits almost overnight, regardless of what that specific country did wrong.

Domestic triggers are self-inflicted. Sudden, poorly sequenced policy changes, an abrupt tax cut with no offsetting spending cut, a currency peg defended well past the point of credibility, an agricultural or industrial policy misstep that guts a major revenue source, can turn a manageable vulnerability into an acute crisis almost by themselves. Political instability compounds both categories: a government seen as unable or unwilling to make hard fiscal choices loses credibility with investors faster than the underlying numbers alone would justify.

body.caption: A Sample of Historical Triggers, by Type

cells: Asian Financial Crisis (1997)
External + Domestic
Short-term dollar debt funding long-term projects, combined with currency pegs that became indefensible once capital reversed
Argentina (2001)
Domestic
A rigid currency board pegging the peso to the dollar collapsed under sustained fiscal deficits it could not accommodate
Eurozone Periphery (2010-12)
External + Domestic
The 2008 global financial crisis exposed years of fiscal slippage and banking-sector fragility in Greece, Portugal, and others
Sri Lanka (2022)
External + Domestic
A tourism collapse during the pandemic met large tax cuts and a sudden fertiliser import ban, covered in full in the next lesson

body.title: Spot the Stage
body.scenario: A country has run a current account deficit above 6% of GDP for three straight years, funded mostly by short-term foreign bank loans and portfolio inflows chasing high interest rates. Its forex reserves currently cover about 2.5 months of imports. Growth has been strong and headline news has been positive throughout this period.
body.prompt: Using the four-stage framework from this lesson, which stage is this country most likely in, and what would you expect to happen if the US Federal Reserve unexpectedly began a rapid rate-hiking cycle?
body.modelAnswer: This country is deep into Stage 1, building vulnerability, with the twin deficit and thin import cover (comfortably under the 3-month danger threshold) both flashing. A rapid Fed hiking cycle is a classic external trigger (Stage 2): the short-term, rate-sensitive foreign capital funding this country's deficits would likely reverse quickly, chasing the newly attractive returns on safe dollar assets. That capital flight would very plausibly push the country into Stage 3, a loss of confidence, with widening spreads, currency depreciation, and further reserve depletion, potentially culminating in the kind of Stage 4 crisis point (capital controls, restructuring, or an IMF programme) this chapter is building toward.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: What does the Greenspan-Guidotti rule specifically test?
options: Whether a country's fiscal deficit is below 3% of GDP
Whether a country's forex reserves are at least equal to its short-term external debt (debt maturing within a year)
Whether a country's credit rating is investment grade
Whether a country's currency is fully convertible
body.explanation: The Greenspan-Guidotti rule, developed after the Asian Financial Crisis, is a rough adequacy test: a country's forex reserves should be enough to cover all of its foreign-currency debt maturing within the next year. It says nothing directly about the fiscal deficit, credit ratings, or currency convertibility, though a country failing this test is usually showing strain across several of those other measures too.

body.text: A sovereign debt crisis is rarely a single event. It is a slow build of vulnerability, met by a trigger, repriced fast by the market, and resolved, one way or another, at a crisis point. Every stage before the last one leaves visible fingerprints in the data, for anyone paying attention.

children.text: The next lesson takes this four-stage anatomy and applies it in full detail to one of the clearest, most recent examples available: Sri Lanka's 2022 default, walked through stage by stage using the exact framework built in this lesson.

points: Sovereign debt crises broadly follow four stages: building vulnerability, a trigger event, a rapid loss of market confidence, and a crisis point where default, restructuring, or emergency measures become unavoidable.

Twin deficits (fiscal plus current account), thin import cover (a commonly cited danger zone is under 3 months), and a debt wall of concentrated near-term maturities are the classic warning signs of building vulnerability.
The Greenspan-Guidotti rule is a widely used reserve adequacy check: forex reserves should at least cover a country's short-term external debt.
Triggers can be external (global rate hikes, commodity shocks, global risk-off events) or domestic (policy missteps, indefensible currency pegs, political instability), and often the two combine.
Vulnerability can look invisible for years under strong headline growth, which is exactly why analysts track the underlying metrics directly rather than relying on the growth narrative alone.

body.text: The thresholds cited in this lesson, including the 3-month import cover benchmark and the Greenspan-Guidotti rule, are widely used rules of thumb, not universal laws, and different institutions apply variations of them. They are useful screening tools, not a substitute for full country-specific analysis.
